Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(The Frisky) -- There exists a school of thought that dictates if you think something catastrophic, then it won't happen. What would happen if my family died in a car accident? What would happen if my house caught on fire? "What makes men connect with the girl of their dreams after sparking with me?" the author asks. Two summers ago, I asked myself: Wouldn't it suck if my first love met someone unexpectedly and got over me before I could begin to move on? Thankfully, my family and my house are safe, but my feelings, my love life, and my ego still need mending. "I met someone." The text message appeared on the screen of my phone and I stopped walking. A group of my friends and I were leaving the movie theater, and it was as if all feelings he had for me were obliterated in one night. We broke up because he was studying in Europe. Poetically, we had expressed our feelings for each other just two nights before. Then he became someone else's boyfriend, and remained so, for much longer than he and I lasted. I should've known it would happen, since it happens quite often. My first kiss, who refused to be my boyfriend, met the girl of his dreams while I still ached for him. They're still together today. Since then, I've been the second choice for several more men. The most recent ones occurred this summer, when I tried and failed to win the heart of my friend Ken -- he started dating the person that he truly liked instead of settling for me. I lost Brian to his ex-girlfriend (although, in that case, I think they belonged together anyway). Each time, I laughed one of those sad, desperate guffaws -- here we go again! What makes men connect with the girl of their dreams after sparking with me? Another concept may be more applicable to my situation: the idea of a self-fulfilling prophecy. Perhaps I'm so aware of my "magic touch" that I'm making it happen. While the first love arrived in Europe, I even warned him what may happen. At the time, though, he waved the thought away. "I'm so picky, I rarely really like a girl like I like you," he typed. A month later, he must've been pleasantly shocked to discover my unfortunate power reached across the Atlantic Ocean. When Ken told me he was dating Mary, I was angry I'd let this happen to me again. I raged at him. He argued that it's irrational to use my past experience to predict the outcome of my future relationships (or my attempts at them). I'm sure that there'll be a guy someday who doesn't find me easy to move on from, but in the meantime I can't ignore the pattern and pretend that each time was a coincidence, as Ken had wanted me to do. I don't know if there is a way to avoid the seemingly inevitable. Each time I let my hopes conquer my superstition, there's a crash, a burn, a deflation, and the temporary loss of the ability to giggle, but I choose the chance of being the girl before the girlfriend over giving up the chance for breaking my streak. outputs.L1:
(The Frisky) — There is a school of thought that holds that if you imagine something catastrophic, it will not happen. What if my family died in a car accident? What if my house caught fire?

“What makes men connect with the girl of their dreams after sparking with me?” the author asks.

Two summers ago, I asked myself: Wouldn’t it be awful if my first love unexpectedly met someone and got over me before I could even begin to move on?

Thankfully, my family and my house are safe. My feelings, my love life, and my ego, however, still need mending.

“I met someone.”

The text message appeared on my phone, and I stopped walking. A group of friends and I were leaving the movie theater, and it felt as though all the feelings he had for me had been obliterated in a single night.

We had broken up because he was studying in Europe. Poetically, we had expressed our feelings for each other just two nights earlier. Then he became someone else’s boyfriend—and remained so for much longer than he and I had lasted.

I should have known it would happen, because it happens quite often. My first kiss, who refused to be my boyfriend, met the girl of his dreams while I was still aching for him. They are still together today.

Since then, I have been the second choice for several more men. The most recent instances occurred this summer, when I tried—and failed—to win the heart of my friend Ken. He began dating the person he truly liked rather than settling for me. I lost Brian to his ex-girlfriend, although, in that case, I think they belonged together anyway.

Each time, I let out one of those sad, desperate guffaws: Here we go again!

What makes men connect with the girl of their dreams after sparking with me?

Another concept may be more applicable to my situation: the self-fulfilling prophecy. Perhaps I am so aware of my “magic touch” that I am making it happen. When my first love arrived in Europe, I even warned him about what might happen. At the time, however, he dismissed the idea.

“I’m so picky. I rarely really like a girl the way I like you,” he typed.

A month later, he must have been pleasantly shocked to discover that my unfortunate power could reach across the Atlantic Ocean.

When Ken told me he was dating Mary, I was furious that I had allowed this to happen to me again. I raged at him. He argued that it was irrational to use my past experiences to predict the outcome of my future relationships—or my attempts at them.

I am sure that someday there will be a guy who does not find it easy to move on from me. In the meantime, however, I cannot ignore the pattern and pretend that each instance was merely a coincidence, as Ken wanted me to do.

I do not know whether there is any way to avoid the seemingly inevitable. Every time I allow my hopes to overcome my superstition, there is a crash, a burn, a deflation, and a temporary loss of my ability to giggle. Still, I choose the possibility of being the girl before the girlfriend over giving up the chance to break my streak.

**(The Frisky) —** One belief holds that imagining a disaster can somehow prevent it from occurring. What if my relatives were killed in a traffic accident? What if my home went up in flames?

The writer wonders, “Why do men seem to find the woman of their dreams after first feeling a connection with me?”

Two summers ago, another dreadful possibility crossed my mind: What if my first love unexpectedly found someone new and moved past our relationship before I had even started recovering?

Fortunately, nothing has happened to my family or my house. My emotions, romantic life, and self-esteem, however, remain damaged.

“I met someone.”

When those words appeared in a text on my phone, I froze in the middle of walking. I was leaving a movie theater with several friends, and it felt as though his feelings for me had disappeared overnight.

Our relationship had ended because he was studying abroad in Europe. In a painfully poetic twist, we had shared our feelings for one another only two nights earlier. Then he became another woman’s boyfriend—and stayed with her far longer than he had been with me.

Perhaps I should have expected it, because this has happened repeatedly. The boy who gave me my first kiss but would not call himself my boyfriend found his ideal woman while I was still longing for him. They remain together today.

After that, several other men also treated me as their backup option. The latest examples happened this summer. I tried unsuccessfully to win over my friend Ken, but rather than settle for me, he began dating the person he genuinely wanted. I also lost Brian when he returned to his former girlfriend, though in their case I believe they were probably meant to be together.

Every time, I let out the same miserable, frantic laugh: Of course this is happening again.

Why do men discover the woman they truly want after sharing a spark with me?

Maybe a different theory better explains my experience: the self-fulfilling prophecy. It is possible that my awareness of this supposed “magic touch” actually helps bring it about.

When my first love reached Europe, I even cautioned him that this might happen. He dismissed the idea at the time.

“I’m extremely selective, and I almost never like a girl as much as I like you,” he wrote.

One month later, he must have been happily surprised to learn that my unlucky influence apparently worked even from across the Atlantic.

When Ken said he had started seeing Mary, I became furious with myself for allowing the same situation to happen once more. I directed that anger at him. He responded that it was unreasonable to assume my future relationships—or attempted relationships—would end a certain way simply because of what had happened before.

I believe that someday I will meet a man who cannot move on from me so easily. Until then, however, I cannot disregard the pattern or act as though every instance was merely accidental, as Ken wanted me to.

I am not sure there is any way to escape what feels unavoidable. Whenever hope overpowers my superstition, the result is another collision, another flameout, another emotional collapse, and a brief inability to laugh.

Even so, I would rather risk being the woman who comes before the girlfriend than surrender the possibility of finally ending this streak.

**TM & © 2009 TMV, Inc. | All Rights Reserved.**

outputs.L4:
For a long time, I believed I had a peculiar role in the romantic lives of men: I was the woman they dated just before meeting the woman they truly wanted.

The pattern seemed too consistent to dismiss. A relationship would begin with excitement and possibility. I would allow myself to imagine that this time might be different, that the man in front of me might choose me fully. Then uncertainty would appear. He would pull away, admit that he was not ready for commitment, or tell me that something was missing. Soon afterward, he would meet someone else and offer her everything he had hesitated to offer me.

Each experience was painful on its own, but together they became a story I told myself. I began to feel like a rehearsal rather than a partner—the person who helped men clarify what they wanted before they found it elsewhere. They seemed to leave our relationships wiser, more emotionally available, and suddenly prepared to commit. Meanwhile, I was left wondering why I had never inspired the same certainty.

The details differed from one relationship to the next. One man insisted that he needed freedom, only to enter a serious relationship shortly after ours ended. Another kept me in an undefined space, close enough to provide affection but never close enough to offer security. When he eventually met someone new, the ambiguity disappeared. He made his intentions clear in a way he never had with me. In another case, I watched a man who had seemed frightened by intimacy become devoted and decisive with someone else.

These experiences did more than break my heart. They changed the way I entered every new relationship.

I became watchful. I looked for signs that I was temporary: a delayed message, a vague answer, a mention of an ex, a reluctance to make plans. Small moments became evidence for a conclusion I had already reached. Even when things were going well, part of me waited for the inevitable revelation that I was not the person he truly wanted.

That expectation created its own problems. Because I feared being rejected, I sometimes concealed what I needed. I tried to appear undemanding, believing that asking for reassurance or commitment would drive someone away. At other times, I did the opposite. I searched for proof of devotion, interpreted uncertainty as abandonment, and reacted to imagined endings before they had occurred.

This is how a self-fulfilling prophecy can operate. A belief influences behavior, and that behavior helps produce the outcome the person fears. If I entered a relationship convinced that I would eventually be replaced, I could not respond only to the man in front of me. I was also responding to every past disappointment. I might choose emotionally unavailable partners because their distance felt familiar. I might accept an unclear relationship because I assumed clarity was too much to ask for. Or I might become so anxious about losing someone that genuine closeness became difficult.

None of this means that I caused other people to mistreat me. Men who were dishonest, avoidant, or unwilling to communicate were responsible for their own choices. Nor does it mean that every failed relationship could have succeeded if I had simply been more confident. Sometimes two people are incompatible. Sometimes feelings are unequal. Sometimes a person really does become ready for commitment only after a relationship has ended.

But recognizing other people’s responsibility does not prevent me from examining my own patterns. If I continually see myself as a second choice, I may tolerate situations that reinforce that identity. I may mistake inconsistency for mystery, emotional distance for complexity, and anxiety for passion. I may remain with someone who is undecided because his hesitation confirms what I already believe about myself.

The most painful realization is not that men have sometimes chosen other women. It is that I may have begun expecting them to do so. The fear became part of my understanding of love. Instead of asking whether a relationship made me feel valued and secure, I focused on proving that I could finally be chosen.

That is a dangerous goal because it places my worth in someone else’s decision. It turns love into a competition and every new partner into a judge. If he stays, I am worthy; if he leaves, my worst beliefs are confirmed.

Breaking the pattern requires a different question. Rather than asking, “Will he choose me?” I need to ask, “Do I choose this relationship?” Is this person emotionally available? Does he communicate honestly? Do his actions match his words? Can I express my needs without feeling ashamed of them? Do I feel loved, or am I constantly auditioning for love?

I may never know why certain men were able to commit after being involved with me. Perhaps timing played a role. Perhaps our relationships taught them something. Perhaps the women they met afterward were simply better suited to them. Their choices do not necessarily reveal a deficiency in me.

What I can understand is the effect the pattern had on my own behavior. Repeated heartbreak taught me to expect abandonment, and that expectation shaped whom I trusted, what I accepted, and how I responded to uncertainty. Fear did not merely follow disappointment; it began preparing the ground for more of it.

The way forward is not to guarantee that I will never be rejected again. No one can make that promise. It is to stop treating rejection as proof that I was always destined to be second. I can learn to recognize mutual love, to leave relationships that depend on ambiguity, and to believe that being chosen is not something I must earn through patience, silence, or pain.

Perhaps I was never a stepping stone to someone else’s ideal partner. Perhaps I was simply a person moving through a series of imperfect relationships, carrying an old wound from one into the next. If so, the pattern is not a fate. It is a story—and stories can be rewritten.
